title: Theatre Chapbooks At Scale: A Statistical Comparative Analysis of Typography
summary: We propose a statistical methodology that quantifies the similarity of typefaces between printed historical books. This provides a tool that accelerates philological analysis. Using character prototypes derived from clustering and aligning automatically extracted character images, the method defines a typeface distance between any two books. To produce actionable outputs, we develop an a contrario statistical framework to interpret the significance of the computed typeface distances. We apply the method to the philological study of 17 th -century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks in a quantity that exceeds the capabilities of systematic visual inspection by human experts. Our method enables the automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types extracted from different books. After validation by human experts, our method has led to new printer attributions being discovered, and former printer attributions being revised. This success strongly suggests that our method has the potential to enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than was previously possible.

AI.tldr: A statistical method for quantifying typeface similarity between printed historical books, using character prototypes from clustered and aligned character images, with an a contrario framework for significance testing. Applied to 17th-century Spanish theatre chapbooks, it enabled automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types, leading to new and revised printer attributions validated by human experts.
AI.motivation: Philological analysis of historical printed books requires identifying which printer produced which book based on typeface. Systematic visual inspection by human experts is infeasible at large scale (e.g., thousands of 17th-century Spanish chapbooks), so an automated, statistically rigorous method for typeface comparison is needed.
AI.method: (1) Automatically extract character images from books; (2) cluster and align them to form character prototypes; (3) define a typeface distance between any two books based on these prototypes; (4) use an a contrario statistical framework to interpret the significance of computed distances; (5) enable comparison of both Roman and Italic typefaces across books.
AI.result: Applied to a large-scale corpus of 17th-century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks beyond human inspection capacity. After validation by human experts, the method led to new printer attributions being discovered and former printer attributions being revised.
AI.conclusion: The successful validation by experts suggests the method can enable digital bibliography at a significantly larger scale than previously possible, accelerating philological analysis through automated typeface comparison.

title: OVEarth-Bench: Evaluating Category Breadth and Query Diversity for Open-Vocabulary Earth Observation
summary: Open-vocabulary Earth observation (EO) aims to localize geospatial concepts specified in natural language rather than a fixed label set. Existing benchmarks, however, usually cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms. To fill this gap, we introduce OVEarth-Bench, which extends existing evaluation in two directions: category breadth, through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive and negative expressions, and query diversity, through vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. We evaluate a broad set of general and EO-specific methods. The evaluation reveals that: (1) the performance of current methods remains limited, while broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; and (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods. These findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation. Our data and evaluation package are released at https://earth-insights.github.io/OVEarth-bench.

AI.tldr: OVEarth-Bench is a new benchmark for open-vocabulary Earth observation that extends existing evaluation along category breadth (broad hierarchical categories with positive/negative expressions) and query diversity (vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries), supporting both mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. Evaluations show current methods perform limitedly, MLLM-based methods are strongest overall, and EO-specific methods generally underperform general models.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary EO benchmarks suffer from narrow category vocabularies and limited query forms, preventing reliable evaluation of geospatial concept localization from natural language.
AI.method: Introduces OVEarth-Bench, a benchmark extending evaluation through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive/negative expressions and diverse query types (vocabulary, referring, reasoning). It provides a unified zero-shot protocol supporting both mask and box localization, and evaluates a range of general and EO-specific methods.
AI.result: (1) Current methods perform limitedly overall, with broader category coverage yielding more stable rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve strongest overall performance; (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest approaches.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and emphasize the need for more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation.

title: VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing
summary: The rise of powerful, accessible image-editing models such as FLUX.2 has brought high-fidelity editing within broad reach. Their capabilities now extend beyond localized modifications to extracting and recontextualizing objects and identities in entirely new scenes. By allowing prompt and generation tokens to attend directly to reference-image tokens, modern models blur the boundary between conventional editing and text-to-image synthesis. This expanded generative freedom also broadens the space of potential misuse, as harmful transformations are no longer confined to a predictable set of localized edits. Existing anti-edit defenses are designed to disrupt the semantic bottleneck of the reference-image encoding in legacy diffusion pipelines. However, newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, thereby often circumventing these protections. We therefore introduce VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts this inner mechanism through which modern models read the source image. Additionally, as existing editing benchmarks leave comprehensive recontextualizations largely untested, we introduce VetoBench, which evaluates defenses not only on conventional localized edits but also on broader contextual shifts. Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts the joint-attention mechanism through which modern image-editing models like FLUX.2 read source images, along with VetoBench, a new benchmark evaluating defenses on both localized edits and broader recontextualizations. VETO outperforms existing defenses across two editing models and three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern image-editing models have expanded capabilities beyond localized edits to extracting and recontextualizing objects/identities in entirely new scenes, broadening misuse potential. Existing anti-edit defenses target the semantic bottleneck of legacy diffusion pipelines, but newer editors use joint-attention blocks that circumvent these protections.
AI.method: VETO introduces a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts the joint-attention mechanism through which modern models read source images. The paper also presents VetoBench, a benchmark evaluating defenses on both conventional localized edits and broader contextual shifts.
AI.result: Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: VETO provides a more effective defense against modern image-editing models by targeting their joint-attention mechanism, and VetoBench addresses the gap in evaluating defenses against comprehensive recontextualizations.

title: Bunraku: Turning a Single Illustration into an Editable Live2D Character
summary: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime characters and virtual avatars, representing each character as a stack of RGBA layers driven by per-layer mesh deformation. Despite its wide use in virtual streaming, mobile games, and interactive characters, authoring a Live2D model still demands weeks of manual layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing, and no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end. We present the first system that, from a single illustration, generates all the structured information a Live2D runtime consumes: ordered RGBA layers, a deformation mesh per layer, and the parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets that make the character move. Stage 1 casts layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh for each layer from its alpha channel alone, then predicts the keypose displacement field of all layers jointly: every vertex of every layer is one token, self-attention spans layer boundaries, and each displacement is factorised into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. Joint rather than independent prediction is what makes the result a coherent character instead of separately plausible parts, and is our largest gain; scaling the network 112x yields none. On 50 held-out characters, under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 attains a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Because a layer's mesh derives from its alpha channel, a clothing layer can be re-textured from a natural-language instruction while the mesh and predicted animation are reused byte-for-byte. We further contribute Live2D-Bench, the first standardized benchmark for the task, and an 8,884-model Live2D corpus with layer and animation supervision.

AI.tldr: Introduces the first end-to-end system that generates a complete Live2D model—ordered RGBA layers, deformation meshes, and parameter-driven keypose offsets—directly from a single illustration, plus a new benchmark (Live2D-Bench) and an 8,884-model corpus.
AI.motivation: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime and avatars, but authoring a model requires weeks of manual work (layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, keyframing). No prior generative method produces the full structured Live2D asset end-to-end.
AI.method: Stage 1 performs layered decomposition via a layered diffusion process using a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh per layer from its alpha channel, then jointly predicts keypose displacement fields for all layers using self-attention that spans layer boundaries, factorizing each displacement into a bounded direction and log-magnitude.
AI.result: On 50 held-out characters with true generation (no teacher forcing), Stage 2 achieves a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Joint prediction is the largest gain; scaling the network 112x yields no improvement. Re-texturing of clothing layers via natural language works while reusing meshes and animations byte-for-byte.
AI.conclusion: Joint prediction across layers, rather than independent prediction, is key to producing a coherent animated character. The system enables downstream capabilities like language-driven re-texturing, and the contributed benchmark and corpus support future research.

title: Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation for Unpaired Cross-Modal Medical Classification
summary: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can transfer diagnostic knowledge from a strong but costly teacher modality to a cheaper and more deployable student modality. In medical image analysis, however, the two modalities are often unpaired: they are collected from different patient cohorts and occupy geometrically incompatible feature spaces. This makes instance-level distillation invalid and direct feature matching unreliable. To address these challenges, we propose Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation (SSCD), which compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook. Each image is represented as a distribution over a common, modality-agnostic vocabulary, and knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions across modalities, both globally and class-conditionally, without requiring paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is evolved online by exponential moving average and kept diverse through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. At inference, all teacher-side and codebook modules are discarded, leaving only the student encoder and classifier. On two heterogeneous unpaired settings, OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/DillanImans/SSCD-unpaired-distillation

AI.tldr: SSCD transfers diagnostic knowledge from a strong teacher modality to a cheaper student modality via a shared discrete semantic codebook, enabling unpaired cross-modal distillation in medical imaging. It aligns global and class-conditional codebook distributions without requiring paired samples, improving student performance on OCT-to-fundus and CT-to-chest-X-ray tasks.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal knowledge distillation faces a critical challenge in medical imaging: teacher and student modalities are often unpaired (collected from different cohorts) and occupy geometrically incompatible feature spaces, making instance-level distillation and direct feature matching invalid or unreliable.
AI.method: SSCD represents each image as a distribution over a shared, modality-agnostic discrete codebook. Knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions across modalities both globally and class-conditionally, without paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is updated online via exponential moving average, with entropy regularization and dead-code restart to maintain diversity. At inference, teacher and codebook modules are discarded, leaving only the student encoder and classifier.
AI.result: On OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1. On CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, it improves from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1. It outperforms all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings.
AI.conclusion: Shared semantic codebook distillation provides an effective framework for unpaired cross-modal knowledge transfer in medical imaging, demonstrating that aligning modality-agnostic semantic distributions is a viable alternative to instance-level or raw feature matching.

title: PanDent: Toward Comprehensive Tooth-Level Structure-Language Consistency in Dental Radiology
summary: Accurate evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography (orthopantomogram, OPG) is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation. This work introduces PanDent, a large-scale, clinically grounded OPG benchmark built upon fine-grained, expert-validated tooth-level annotations. The dataset comprises 9,524 high-quality OPGs, each associated with comprehensive structured annotations produced by experienced dentists and further validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist, providing clinically reliable supervision for tooth-level diagnosis and reasoning. Clinically consistent radiology reports are constructed from expert-validated findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. This design enables evaluation of whether MLLMs generate reports that are not only linguistically coherent but also clinically consistent with expert-validated tooth-level findings. Experiments are conducted on diverse MLLMs, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) proprietary models, general-domain open-source models, and medical-specific models. Results show that current MLLMs can generate fluent reports, yet fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, exhibiting substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, substantially enhancing visual localization accuracy and diagnostic correctness, and bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation. These results establish PanDent as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI.

AI.tldr: PanDent is a large-scale, clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs in dental panoramic radiography, comprising 9,524 expert-validated OPGs with fine-grained tooth-level annotations and clinically consistent radiology reports. It reveals that current MLLMs produce fluent but clinically inconsistent reports, with fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and clinical consistency.
AI.motivation: Evaluating MLLMs in dental panoramic radiography is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation, making it difficult to assess whether models can perform tooth-level diagnosis and reasoning accurately.
AI.method: PanDent is constructed with 9,524 high-quality OPGs with expert-validated tooth-level annotations by dentists and validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist. Clinically consistent radiology reports are generated from structured findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured evidence and free-text descriptions. Diverse MLLMs (SOTA proprietary, general open-source, and medical-specific models) are evaluated, and fine-tuning is performed on PanDent.
AI.result: Current MLLMs can generate fluent reports but fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, with substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, visual localization accuracy, and diagnostic correctness, bringing outputs closer to expert dental interpretation.
AI.conclusion: PanDent serves as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI.

title: VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System
summary: Text-to-video models have achieved remarkable visual quality, yet they still struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because the temporal evolution of a scene must be inferred implicitly from a highly compressed text prompt. Existing chain-of-thought approaches introduce intermediate plans or visual states, but these representations are typically non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process. To address this limitation, we introduce VideoCoCo, an agentic dual-engine framework in which executable Blender code serves as a process-level chain of thought. Given a text prompt, a coding agent synthesizes a Blender program that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution. The executable simulation engine runs the program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, which is subsequently transformed into a photorealistic video by a generative video engine through draft-conditioned editing. This decomposition separates process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization. To adapt the video editor to simulated drafts, we construct VideoCoCo-3K, a curated dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets. VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks. These results demonstrate that executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation.

AI.tldr: VideoCoCo is an agentic dual-engine framework for physically consistent text-to-video generation that uses executable Blender code as a process-level chain of thought. A coding agent synthesizes a Blender program specifying scene dynamics, a simulation engine renders a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, and a generative video engine transforms the draft into photorealistic video. It achieves state-of-the-art results on PhyGenBench (0.558 vs 0.475 baseline) and VBench-2.0 (77.88 vs 52.18 baseline).
AI.motivation: Text-to-video models struggle with physically consistent dynamics because temporal scene evolution must be implicitly inferred from compressed text prompts. Existing chain-of-thought approaches use intermediate plans or visual states that are typically non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process.
AI.method: VideoCoCo is a dual-engine framework: (1) A coding agent synthesizes executable Blender code from a text prompt that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution (process-level chain of thought). (2) A simulation engine executes the Blender program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft. (3) A generative video engine transforms the draft into a photorealistic video via draft-conditioned editing. To adapt the video editor to simulated drafts, a curated dataset VideoCoCo-3K of draft-instruction-target triplets is constructed.
AI.result: VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation, as it separates process-level reasoning (simulation) from high-fidelity visual realization (generative rendering).

title: IGME: Efficient Chained Method Ensemble for Transferable Semantic Segmentation Attacks
summary: Semantic segmentation models are vulnerable to transferable adversarial perturbations, yet evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction models can be computationally expensive. Existing ensemble attacks often rely on multiple surrogate models, increasing the computation cost, even harder for segmentation. This paper studies an efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation. We formulate transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, allowing the expensive source-model gradient computation to be shared. To reduce the update instability introduced by chained composition, we further use an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction as an empirical stabilization heuristic. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes evaluate the resulting transferability efficiency trade-off across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models. IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IGME, an efficient single-source attack method for transferable adversarial perturbations on semantic segmentation. It formulates transferable attack composition as chained computation over differentiable attack components to share expensive gradient computations, and uses integrated-gradient-style path-averaged directions for stabilization. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes show competitive transferability vs. single-source baselines with favorable runtime vs. ensemble attacks using only one source model.
AI.motivation: Evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction models is computationally expensive, and existing ensemble attacks requiring multiple surrogate models increase computation cost even further. An efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation is needed.
AI.method: The method (1) formulates transferable attack composition as chained computation over differentiable attack components, enabling shared gradient computation from a single source model; (2) uses an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction to reduce update instability from chained composition as an empirical stabilization heuristic.
AI.result: On Pascal VOC and Cityscapes, IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.
AI.conclusion: IGME demonstrates that efficient transferable attacks on semantic segmentation are achievable with a single source model by sharing gradient computation and stabilizing chained updates, offering a practical trade-off between transferability and efficiency.

title: ProgFormer: Hierarchical Voxel Diffusion Transformer for Longitudinal Brain MRI Prediction
summary: Predicting future structural MRI of a brain is challenging because longitudinal changes are often subtle and confined to specific anatomical regions, while most subject-specific brain structure remains stable over time. An effective model should therefore preserve global brain structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression. Existing latent-space-based methods improve computational efficiency, but suffer from information loss during their compression-reconstruction procedure. In contrast, direct voxel-space methods avoid latent reconstruction but commonly use a unified prediction pathway to model brain structure and progression-related changes. Subtle local changes may therefore be overshadowed by the dominant stable brain structure. To address these challenges, we propose ProgFormer, a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction. ProgFormer uses a coarse pathway to perform the primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens. This pathway models overall brain structure and longitudinal context. The fine pathway then uses the coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. The two pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space through conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separately learned image autoencoder. The predicted future scan is then generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the estimated velocity field over a sequence of Euler steps. Extensive experimental results on three widely used benchmarks, ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS, under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favourable performance compared against several state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction. It uses a coarse pathway for global volumetric prediction and a fine pathway for voxel-level refinement, jointly estimating a velocity field via conditional flow matching directly in voxel space—avoiding latent-space information loss. It outperforms SOTA methods on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal brain MRI prediction is challenging because changes are subtle and localized while most brain structure remains stable. Existing latent-space methods lose information via compression-reconstruction, and direct voxel-space methods use a unified pathway where dominant stable structures overshadow fine-grained disease progression changes.
AI.method: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer with two pathways: (1) a coarse pathway performs primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens, modeling overall brain structure and longitudinal context; (2) a fine pathway uses coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within patches. The pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space via conditional flow matching, without a separately learned image autoencoder. Prediction is generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the velocity field over Euler steps.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three benchmarks (ADNI, AIBL, OASIS) under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favorable performance compared against several state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: ProgFormer effectively preserves global brain structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression by decoupling coarse and fine modeling pathways, avoiding latent-space information loss, and enabling end-to-end prediction directly in voxel space.

title: Drawing-Recode: Annotation Grounding for Parametric CAD Code Generation from Raster 2D CAD Drawings
summary: Recovering Parametric CAD sequences from raster-format 2D Computer-Aided Design (CAD) drawings accumulated prior to digital transformation is important for part reproduction and manufacturing process automation. However, existing studies either process only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, limiting their use of dimensional information for 3D Parametric CAD sequences recovery. We propose Drawing-Recode, a framework that generates Parametric CAD sequences as CAD code from raster 2D CAD drawings. Drawing-Recode extracts geometric features via an image encoder and recognizes annotations through a separate text recognition module, then explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information using cross-attention and our proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL). The resulting features are fed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format. Experiments show that Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions. We expect Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings and to part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

AI.tldr: Drawing-Recode is a framework that recovers Parametric CAD sequences as CAD code from raster 2D CAD drawings by combining an image encoder for geometric features, a text recognition module for annotations, cross-attention with an Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL) to link annotations to geometry, and an LLM to generate code in SPCC format. It outperforms baselines and is robust on scanned drawings for industrial applications.
AI.motivation: Recovering Parametric CAD sequences from raster 2D CAD drawings is important for part reproduction and manufacturing automation, but existing methods only handle vector drawings or specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information.
AI.method: Drawing-Recode extracts geometric features via an image encoder, recognizes annotations via a separate text recognition module, explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information using cross-attention and a proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL), and feeds the resulting features into an LLM to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format.
AI.result: Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions.
AI.conclusion: Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings, supporting part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

title: Inference-Time Agentic Decision Rules Beat Longer Evolving Search for Multi-Image Medical Reasoning
comment: Presented at the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Multi-Modal Reasoning for Agentic Intelligence
summary: Multi-image medical VQA is not merely a prompt-length problem; it is a fundamental challenge of agentic decision-making. Medical vision-language agents must aggregate evidence across ordered images, remain robust to answer-order perturbations, and avoid overfitting to noisy search-time feedback. We study MedFrameQA through a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies, optimized using the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration and evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test). Across five independent repeated runs, the strongest method emerges as the simplest robust aggregator: the \textbf{order-vote} policy achieves $57.89 \pm 0.65\%$ final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline ($52.73 \pm 0.42\%$) and the more complex, albeit brittle, order-rerank variant ($55.79 \pm 0.43\%$). Paired bootstrap analysis confirms these significant gains. Extending the evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: while holdout performance marginally increases, final-test accuracy drops from $57.89\%$ to $56.02\%$. Our findings suggest that for multi-image medical reasoning, defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget.

AI.tldr: This paper studies MedFrameQA, a multi-image medical VQA task, comparing five inference-time agentic strategies. The simplest method, order-vote, achieves the best final-test accuracy (57.89% ± 0.65%), outperforming both the fixed baseline and a more complex order-rerank variant. Increasing evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations does not improve generalization, suggesting that defining the correct agentic decision rule matters more than expanding optimization budget.
AI.motivation: Multi-image medical VQA requires more than just handling long prompts—it demands agentic decision-making capabilities. Current approaches may overfit to noisy search-time feedback, be sensitive to answer-order perturbations, and lack robustness in aggregating evidence across ordered images.
AI.method: A controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies optimized with the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration. Evaluations were conducted on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test) with five independent repeated runs, and paired bootstrap analysis for statistical significance.
AI.result: The order-vote policy achieves 57.89% ± 0.65% final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline (52.73% ± 0.42%) and order-rerank variant (55.79% ± 0.43%). Extending evolutionary search from 50 to 100 generations decreases final-test accuracy from 57.89% to 56.02%, despite marginal holdout improvements.
AI.conclusion: For multi-image medical reasoning, selecting the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget. Simplicity and robustness in aggregation strategy outperform more complex but brittle alternatives.

title: Objective-Aligned Direct Answer SFT for Robust Multi-Frame Medical VQA
comment: Presented at the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Multimodal Foundation Models for Biomedicine: Challenges and Opportunities
summary: Multi-frame medical VQA appears to reward increasingly complex adaptation: controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, and staged continuation all appear plausible from first principles. We test a simpler competing hypothesis on MedFrameQA: methods that remain tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest \emph{robust} adaptation family once evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. We compare controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The strongest robust family is direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Empirically, this family yields substantial improvements in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining remarkably stable across repeated seeds and matched controls, ensuring our claims reflect true family-level robustness rather than an isolated hyperparameter peak. Furthermore, post-hoc calibration effectively repairs confidence estimation without compromising accuracy, and the core approach transfers consistently to secondary backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The main result is therefore not that a complex auxiliary mechanism wins, but that objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family we found for MedFrameQA. By establishing this strong, minimalist baseline, we hope to redirect community focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

AI.tldr: Direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B is the strongest robust adaptation family for MedFrameQA, outperforming complex alternatives like controller-based methods and staged continuation, while remaining stable across seeds and transferring to other backbones.
AI.motivation: The field of multi-frame medical VQA tends toward increasingly complex adaptations (controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, hard-negative mixing, staged continuation). The authors challenge this trend by testing a simpler hypothesis: methods tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest robust family once evaluation is properly controlled.
AI.method: The authors systematically compared controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on MedFrameQA. Evaluation was controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration.
AI.result: Direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B emerged as the strongest robust family, yielding substantial gains in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining stable across repeated seeds. Post-hoc calibration improved confidence estimation without sacrificing accuracy, and the approach transferred to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.conclusion: Complex auxiliary mechanisms do not win; objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family. The authors establish a minimalist baseline and advocate redirecting community focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

title: ZMIS-SAM: Segment Anything Model Enhanced with Wavelet Transform for Zooplankton Microscopy Image Instance Segmentation
summary: As primary consumers in the marine food chain, zooplankton play a crucial role in maintaining marine ecological balance. However, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibits limited performance in microscopic image instance segmentation due to its lack of zooplankton-specific domain knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a novel instance segmentation model based on SAM and wavelet transform (ZMIS-SAM), effectively tackling issues such as inaccurate classification, discontinuous segmentation of slender appendages, and incomplete boundary segmentation. Our framework incorporates three core innovations: ZM-ViT enhances SAM's capability to model zooplankton morphology and image intensity distributions through two lightweight adapters, the Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM) improves continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages by integrating general-purpose and domain-specific features, and the Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module effectively recovers high-frequency details to refine boundary segmentation completeness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and exhibits strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.

AI.tldr: ZMIS-SAM is a SAM-based instance segmentation model with wavelet transforms designed for zooplankton microscopic images, addressing SAM's limitations in domain-specific tasks through three innovations: ZM-ViT adapters for domain adaptation, NFAM for continuous segmentation of slender appendages, and WM2FE for boundary refinement via wavelet-based multi-scale enhancement.
AI.motivation: SAM lacks zooplankton-specific domain knowledge, resulting in poor performance on microscopic image instance segmentation tasks, including inaccurate classification, discontinuous segmentation of slender appendages, and incomplete boundary segmentation.
AI.method: The framework integrates three core innovations: (1) ZM-ViT with two lightweight adapters to enhance SAM's modeling of zooplankton morphology and intensity distributions, (2) NFAM (Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module) to improve continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages by merging general and domain-specific features, and (3) WM2FE (Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement) to recover high-frequency details for complete boundary segmentation.
AI.result: ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and demonstrates strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ZMIS-SAM effectively overcomes SAM's limitations in zooplankton microscopic image segmentation, providing accurate and complete instance segmentation with robust cross-domain generalization.

title: MeshFM: 2D Features Are All You Need for 3D Shape Understanding
summary: We present MeshFM, an efficient feedforward framework for extracting rich features from 3D inputs. Our method distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D. We train a feedforward network to directly predict 3D features without requiring optimization during inference. The approach utilizes a two-stage training strategy. First, we optimize a feature field in 3D using only 2D feature supervision. Second, we train a network to regress this feature field. The entire procedure requires no 3D annotation, instead relying on the powerful information in 2D foundation models. We demonstrate that our learned features can be immediately applied to downstream tasks, including part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation. Extensive experiments show that MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, performs on par with methods trained explicitly with 3D supervision, even without task-specific fine-tuning. Moreover, our model is trained to be robust to extreme rotations of the input objects. Project page: https://threedle.github.io/MeshFM/

AI.tldr: MeshFM is a feedforward framework that distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D features for meshes, using a two-stage training strategy (optimizing a feature field with 2D supervision, then training a network to regress it) without requiring 3D annotations. The learned features work on downstream tasks like part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation, performing on par with 3D-supervised methods.
AI.motivation: To efficiently extract rich 3D features without expensive per-sample optimization during inference and without requiring 3D annotations, leveraging the powerful representations already learned by 2D foundation models.
AI.method: A two-stage strategy: (1) optimize a 3D feature field using only 2D feature supervision from foundation models, and (2) train a feedforward network to regress this feature field. The model is trained for robustness to extreme rotations and requires no 3D annotation.
AI.result: Learned features perform on par with methods trained with explicit 3D supervision on part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation, without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: 2D foundation model features can be effectively distilled into 3D via feedforward prediction, enabling immediate application to downstream tasks with no 3D labels and competitive performance.

title: MPIE-Bench: Benchmarking Anatomically Plausible Multi-Person Interaction Editing
summary: Text-to-image and personalized editing models now synthesize high-fidelity single-subject images with ease. Yet placing multiple named people into shared contact actions such as embrace, carry, or grapple still exposes major failures: fused limbs, invented extremities, and interpenetrating bodies. Existing evaluations largely overlook these anatomical and geometric issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists often saturate on Interaction while the errors remain obvious to humans. We introduce MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample benchmark of video-mined editing triplets spanning 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities (C0-C3). We also propose MPIE-Eval, whose two new axes score contact-time geometry from a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction. Anatomy asks whether every human-like mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies, and Interaction asks whether the penetration and surface distance between those bodies match the contact the instruction asked for. Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models, so no single editor is strong on both, while VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study confirms that both axes track human judgement more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and the rankings hold under ablation of every weight and threshold.

AI.tldr: MPIE-Bench is a 2,500-sample benchmark for multi-person image editing, with MPIE-Eval using mesh reconstruction to evaluate anatomy and interaction quality, revealing that current editors and VLM judges significantly overestimate performance on multi-person contact interactions.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image and personalized editing models excel at single-subject generation but fail on multi-person contact interactions (embrace, carry, grapple), producing fused limbs and interpenetrating bodies. Existing evaluations miss these geometric/anatomical issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists saturate on interaction quality while errors remain visible to humans, necessitating a better benchmark and evaluation method.
AI.method: The paper introduces MPIE-Bench (2,500 samples, 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, 4 contact densities C0-C3) mined from videos, and MPIE-Eval which scores two axes via frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction: Anatomy (whether human-like masses are explained by complete reconstructed bodies) and Interaction (whether penetration and surface distance between bodies match the requested contact).
AI.result: Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models—no single editor excels at both—while VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study confirms both axes track human judgment more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and rankings are stable under ablations of every weight and threshold.
AI.conclusion: Current editors significantly underperform on multi-person contact editing despite high VLM scores, and the proposed mesh-based evaluation axes provide a more reliable, human-aligned assessment that exposes these failures.

title: MedXplore: Towards Reliable and Unbiased Generalized Category Discovery in Medical Imaging
summary: Deep learning has shown strong potential in medical image analysis, but most existing methods rely on large-scale annotations and a closed-world assumption that rarely holds in clinical practice. Although Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) has advanced rapidly on natural images, it remains underexplored in medical imaging. To address this issue, we propose MedXplore, a unified framework for reliable and unbiased medical GCD, optimizing from both perceptual and decision levels. Specifically, at the perceptual level, taking a frequency domain perspective, Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to not only highlight local abnormal signals relative to the global context, but also provide reliable semantic anchors for patch consistency learning. At the decision level, Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Together, the two modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average \textbf{8.5\%} gain in \textit{All} accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On Kvasir, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50\% to 0.80\%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.

AI.tldr: MedXplore is a unified framework for Generalized Category Discovery in medical imaging, addressing annotation scarcity and closed-world limitations through frequency-domain perceptual learning and adaptive decision-level margins, achieving 8.5% average accuracy gains and reducing false-old errors from 14.50% to 0.80%.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning medical image analysis methods depend on large-scale annotations and closed-world assumptions that fail in clinical practice. Although GCD has advanced on natural images, it remains unexplored in medical imaging, leaving a gap for handling novel/unseen categories in medical data.
AI.method: MedXplore optimizes at two levels: (1) Perceptual level - Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to highlight abnormal signals and provide semantic anchors for patch consistency learning; (2) Decision level - Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins based on semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability.
AI.result: Achieves an average 8.5% gain in All accuracy over the strongest baselines across multiple benchmarks. On Kvasir, reduces false-old errors dramatically from 14.50% to 0.80%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: The two complementary modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias, making medical GCD more reliable and unbiased for clinical deployment.

title: BlindPSNR: A No-Reference Fidelity Predictor for Low-Light Image Enhancement
summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) methods involve tunable parameters that are typically fixed, often leading to performance degradation when applied across scenes. Manually selecting the best configuration, however, can be time-consuming and not always practical. Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is the natural fidelity criterion for automating parameter selection, yet it requires a ground-truth reference that is typically unavailable. To our knowledge, no learning-based method addresses no-reference PSNR prediction for low-light image enhancement; the natural surrogate, no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA), targets perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity, and all seven baselines we test achieve 0% top-1 selection accuracy on our benchmark. With paired training data, the ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network. Building on this, we propose BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression. While a scalar-regression baseline achieves top-1 accuracy of 54.4%, BlindPSNR raises this to 89.5% with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets (SRCC = 0.61-0.67).

AI.tldr: Proposes BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that predicts PSNR for low-light image enhancement parameter selection using windowed cross-attention and heteroscedastic regression, achieving 89.5% top-1 accuracy versus 54.4% for scalar regression baselines.
AI.motivation: Low-light image enhancement methods have tunable parameters that are typically fixed, causing performance degradation across scenes. Manual parameter selection is time-consuming, and PSNR-based automation requires ground-truth references that are unavailable. Existing no-reference IQA methods target perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity and fail entirely (0% top-1 accuracy) for this task.
AI.method: BlindPSNR fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression. Training uses paired data where ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network.
AI.result: BlindPSNR achieves 89.5% top-1 selection accuracy (vs. 54.4% for scalar regression baseline) with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets with SRCC of 0.61-0.67.
AI.conclusion: BlindPSNR demonstrates that no-reference PSNR prediction is feasible for automating parameter selection in low-light image enhancement, dramatically improving selection accuracy and generalization over existing approaches including NR-IQA baselines.

title: 4DHumanDiff: Direct Text-to-4DGS Generation for Consistent 360-Degree Dynamic Humans
summary: Generating high-quality 360-degree dynamic human assets from text prompts is challenging. Existing methods usually synthesize monocular or multi-view videos first and then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and often causes incomplete geometry or view-inconsistent renderings. We present 4DHumanDiff, a diffusion framework that directly generates dynamic humans represented by 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) from text prompts. By modeling the structured 4D representation space end-to-end, 4DHumanDiff avoids video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction, making it better suited for view-consistent and temporally coherent asset generation. The model uses a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation. We further construct a large-scale text-to-4DGS dataset with 60,000 high-quality pairs, and introduce 2D regularization and training-free 4D interpolation to improve rendering quality and motion smoothness. Experiments show that 4DHumanDiff generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.

AI.tldr: 4DHumanDiff is a diffusion framework that directly generates dynamic 360-degree human assets as 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) representations from text prompts, eliminating the need for video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction. It uses a 3D U-Net with temporal attention, a 60,000-pair text-to-4DGS dataset, 2D regularization, and training-free 4D interpolation to achieve view-consistent, temporally coherent outputs in under one minute—10x faster than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for generating 360-degree dynamic humans from text rely on synthesizing monocular or multi-view videos first, then fitting a 4D representation. This pipeline is expensive, often produces incomplete geometry, and suffers from view-inconsistent renderings.
AI.method: 4DHumanDiff directly models the structured 4D Gaussian Splatting representation space end-to-end using a diffusion framework. It employs a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation, is trained on a large-scale dataset of 60,000 text-to-4DGS pairs, and incorporates 2D regularization and training-free 4D interpolation to enhance rendering quality and motion smoothness.
AI.result: 4DHumanDiff generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency compared to existing approaches, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.
AI.conclusion: Directly generating 4D representations (rather than reconstructing them from videos) is a more efficient and higher-quality paradigm for text-driven dynamic human asset generation, offering significant speedups and improved consistency.

title: MMOOC: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Out-of-Context Evaluation in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks, but often fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. A reliable MLLM should refuse truly out-of-context (OOC) questions with subject-level context shifts while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions with non-subject context shifts. Existing benchmarks mainly target OOC or visually unanswerable questions, but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shifts. To fill this gap, we present MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating refusal and robust answering abilities of MLLMs. MMOOC contains over 41K image-question pairs, including answerable Shifted IC cases and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types and six visual scenarios, with data quality ensured through MLLM-based filtering and human verification. We evaluate model responses using Accuracy and Refusal Rate, and further introduce an LLM-as-a-Judge metric to assess the correctness of model reasoning. Experiments on diverse MLLMs show that current models still struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. We further analyze key failure patterns and show that post-training can improve robustness. MMOOC will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: MMOOC is a large-scale benchmark (41K+ image-question pairs) for evaluating MLLMs' ability to refuse out-of-context (OOC) questions while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions, covering eight shift types, three question formats, and six visual scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on OOC or visually unanswerable questions but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shift types, while reliable MLLMs need to distinguish between subject-level context shifts (should refuse) and non-subject context shifts (should answer).
AI.method: The authors construct MMOOC with over 41K image-question pairs including answerable Shifted IC and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types and six visual scenarios. Data quality is ensured via MLLM-based filtering and human verification. They evaluate models with Accuracy, Refusal Rate, and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric for reasoning correctness.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse MLLMs show current models struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. Key failure patterns are analyzed, and post-training is shown to improve robustness.
AI.conclusion: MMOOC fills a gap in evaluating MLLMs' refusal and robust answering abilities under diverse context shifts, and will be made publicly available to support future research.

title: Learning Color Grading, No Photo Sharing: Federated Aesthetic Preference Learning for Personalized Image Enhancement
summary: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, yet learning such preferences commonly depends on private photos and ratings that are unsuitable for centralized collection. The task must infer preference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback and translate it into natural-looking color transformations on resource-constrained user devices. We introduce FedPAIE, a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework for user-adaptive color grading without centralizing raw photos or ratings. FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance. Training remains lightweight throughout the pipeline: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity. FedPAIE thus connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches.

AI.tldr: FedPAIE is a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework that trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer and a CLUT enhancer entirely in a decentralized manner, learning user preferences without centralizing private photos or ratings.
AI.motivation: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, but learning such preferences typically requires private photos and ratings that cannot be centrally collected. The task is challenging due to sparse, heterogeneous feedback and the need for efficient, on-device color transformations without paired user retouches.
AI.method: FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer in a federated setting, calibrates it into a personalized scorer using a small local support set, then freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty prevent proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance.
AI.result: Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity. The pipeline is lightweight: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer.
AI.conclusion: FedPAIE connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches, enabling privacy-preserving, resource-constrained personalized image enhancement.

title: Witness Evidence Portfolios: Single-Prefill Risk Detection for Closed Multimodal Answers
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures; includes supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/SouthWinter/WEP
summary: Reliable deployment of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system. Confidence scores capture candidate margins, but not where the estimated signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed. We study inference-time risk detection for closed visual answers using the same white-box prefill path that produces the answer. Witness Evidence Portfolios (WEP) first estimates, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes these contributions through two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation chooses the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. WEP needs no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier. Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model--dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs. WEP targets white-box closed-answer systems and uses a labeled calibration slice.

AI.tldr: WEP is an inference-time risk detection method for MLLMs that estimates layer-by-layer visual evidence contributions (supporting or contradicting the predicted answer) from the white-box prefill path, then summarizes them into interpretable evidence portfolios fused with candidate confidence to decide whether an answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to stronger systems.
AI.motivation: Current confidence scores capture candidate margins but not where the visual readouts come from or how they are distributed, making it difficult to reliably assess whether a confident visual answer should be trusted for deployment.
AI.method: WEP first estimates per-layer visual contributions supporting or contradicting the predicted candidate via the white-box prefill path. It summarizes these into two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation selects the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is then fused with candidate confidence. It requires no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier.
AI.result: Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model-dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs.
AI.conclusion: WEP provides a lightweight, interpretable, and effective inference-time risk detection mechanism for white-box MLLMs with closed visual answers, using labeled calibration slices.

title: JigShape: Evaluating Visual-Geometric Reasoning in VLMs through Jigsaw Puzzles
summary: Jigsaw puzzle solving requires jointly reasoning about visual content and geometric constraints, yet existing benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions. We introduce \textit{\ours{}}, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements that, combined with visual content, yield unambiguous ground truth. Across 95K instances at four grid densities (4$\times$4 to 16$\times$16), we find that \textbf{zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning}: only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4$\times$4 puzzles, while all others perform at chance level. While supervised fine-tuning achieves $>$97\% on 4$\times$4, \textbf{all models collapse on larger grids}: GPT-5.5 drops from 70\% to near-random on 8$\times$8, and even fine-tuned models fall below 5\% on 12$\times$12. This ``scaling cliff'' suggests current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of pieces increases. \ours{} establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces JigsawBench, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking jigsaw pieces that provide unambiguous ground truth through geometric constraints. Testing 95K instances across various grid sizes, they find that zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning (only GPT-5.5 exceeds random baseline on 4x4), and all models—including fine-tuned ones—collapse on larger grids (the "scaling cliff"), establishing scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing jigsaw puzzle benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions, making it difficult to properly evaluate visual-geometric joint reasoning in vision-language models.
AI.method: They introduce a new benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements yielding unambiguous ground truth. The benchmark includes 95K instances at four grid densities (4x4 to 16x16), testing both zero-shot VLMs and fine-tuned models.
AI.result: Only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4x4 puzzles; all others perform at chance level. Supervised fine-tuning achieves >97% on 4x4, but all models collapse on larger grids: GPT-5.5 drops from 70% to near-random on 8x8, and fine-tuned models fall below 5% on 12x12.
AI.conclusion: The "scaling cliff" demonstrates that current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of pieces increases, establishing scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

title: RefineSVG: Visual Feedback-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Image-to-SVG Generation
comment: 17 pages, 5 main-paper figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). Includes the complete supplementary material
summary: We propose RefineSVG, a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction. Existing MLLM-based approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input only once and must generate thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This paradigm inevitably leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images. RefineSVG overcomes this limitation by invoking an external rendering engine after an initial SVG generation pass to compare the rendered output against the target image. The comparison yields a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) that is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal, driving a targeted correction step. To support this render-observe-correct interaction, we further introduce an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary that compresses token sequences by over 52%. A progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning aligns the model with closed-loop visual correction. Extensive experiments show that RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.Code is available at https://github.com/liuxiaobo66/RefineSVG.

AI.tldr: RefineSVG is a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework allowing MLLMs to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation via self-correction, using an external rendering engine and Diff-Map feedback signals.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based image-to-SVG methods use single-pass open-loop inference, suffering from geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images due to lack of intermediate verification.
AI.method: RefineSVG invokes an external rendering engine after initial SVG generation, compares rendered output with target image to produce a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) used as ReAct-style correction signal. It introduces an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary compressing tokens by 52%+ and uses a progressive training pipeline (SFT, rejection-sampling cold-start data, end-to-end agentic RL).
AI.result: RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency on extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop render-observe-correct feedback with efficient token compression and progressive training significantly improves MLLM image-to-SVG generation quality.

title: Calibrate Before Reason: Robust Visual Token Reduction against Semantic Drift in VLMs
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from prohibitive inference overhead due to long sequences of visual tokens. However, existing visual token reduction methods mainly improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens without examining whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original representation. Mapping the original N-token visual sequence to K tokens may discard, dilute, or misassign critical visual cues, triggering severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding. In this paper, we first introduce the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' to visual token reduction and propose CaRe, a training-free robust framework that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs. CaRe consists of two mutually complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors. Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks verify that CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, our method retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance, delivering up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.

AI.tldr: CaRe is a training-free framework for visual token reduction in large Vision-Language Models that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to prevent semantic drift, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while pruning 94.4% of visual tokens and retaining 96.4% of full-token performance with up to 2.30x faster inference.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token reduction methods focus on efficiency via pruning or compression but fail to verify whether reduced representations remain semantically consistent with the originals. Aggressive reduction can discard, dilute, or misassign critical visual cues, causing semantic drift that degrades VLM understanding.
AI.method: CaRe introduces the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' and consists of two complementary modules: (1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which selects stable calibration anchors under multi-directional perturbations; (2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors to preserve semantic fidelity.
AI.result: CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks. It prunes 94.4% of visual tokens while retaining 96.4% of original full-token performance, achieving up to 2.30x faster end-to-end inference relative to unpruned vanilla models.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating compact visual representations before reasoning is an effective and training-free strategy to maintain semantic fidelity in VLMs under aggressive token reduction, offering both efficiency and robustness without requiring retraining.

title: PrintAnything: Learning an Intermediate Representation for 3D printing G-code Generation
summary: Point clouds are one of the most fundamental and widely used 3D representations, serving as the most basic geometric representation of 3D shapes. Nevertheless, most existing 3D printing pipelines require a watertight mesh as input, preventing the direct use of point clouds for fabrication. A common workaround is to reconstruct meshes from point clouds; however, the resulting meshes often contain geometric artifacts, such as incorrect faces or topological inconsistencies, that are difficult to repair and may lead to printing failures. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrintAnything, a novel framework that learns to produce executable 3D printing G-code directly from 3D point clouds without requiring mesh reconstruction. To enable point clouds to serve as direct input for slice-wise toolpath generation, we introduce a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling in 3D printing. To eliminate mesh dependency and provide a unified representation that bridges point clouds and G-code, we propose Geometric plan (G-plan) map, a compact 2D representation composed of occupancy, region, and flow maps that encode the geometric and extrusion properties required for toolpath synthesis in 3D printing. As a result, our proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, enabling a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing. The code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/Sangminhong/PrintAnything}{https://github.com/Sangminhong/PrintAnything}.

AI.tldr: PrintAnything is a novel framework that generates executable 3D printing G-code directly from point clouds, bypassing the need for watertight mesh reconstruction. It introduces a slice-wise point projection strategy and a Geometric plan (G-plan) map—a 2D representation combining occupancy, region, and flow maps—to enable a fully mesh-free 3D printing pipeline.
AI.motivation: Most 3D printing pipelines require watertight meshes, but point clouds—the most fundamental 3D representation—cannot be directly used. Reconstructing meshes from point clouds often produces geometric artifacts (incorrect faces, topological inconsistencies) that are difficult to repair and lead to printing failures. A mesh-free direct approach is needed.
AI.method: The framework proposes two key components: (1) a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with the layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling, and (2) a Geometric plan (G-plan) map—a compact 2D representation composed of occupancy, region, and flow maps—that encodes geometric and extrusion properties required for toolpath synthesis, bridging point clouds and G-code without requiring meshes.
AI.result: The proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, demonstrating a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing.
AI.conclusion: PrintAnything eliminates the mesh dependency in 3D printing pipelines by learning to generate executable G-code directly from point clouds, offering a robust alternative to mesh-reconstruction-based approaches. The code is publicly available.

title: Articulated Object Reconstruction from Rest-State Observation
summary: Building interactive digital twins requires recovering both 3D geometry and the kinematic structures that govern how objects articulate. Yet existing methods for articulated object reconstruction require explicitly observable motion from multiple articulation states. We introduce a rest-state formulation that reconstructs articulated objects from a single closed configuration, an inherently ill-posed setting where geometry, semantics, and motion priors compensate for the absence of motion cues. Our framework adopts an explicit mesh as an intermediate representation for cross-model verification and fusion, reconciling noisy outputs from vision-language and segmentation models into spatially consistent part structures. To estimate joint parameters without observed motion, we use a video diffusion model to synthesize articulation hypotheses and validate them through geometric consistency. Our approach achieves accurate part decomposition and physically plausible articulation, performing competitively with motion-observing reconstruction-based, generation-based, and modular pretrained-model baselines.
